Heat exchangers under API 510: shells, channels and tubes

Short answer: API 510 treats heat exchangers, including air coolers, as pressure vessels. The shell, channel, heads, covers and nozzles therefore fall under the code's inspection intervals, repair rules and inspector oversight. For the exchanger-specific work, API 510 points readers elsewhere: to API RP 572 for inspection practice, to ASME PCC-2 Article 312 for inspecting and repairing shell-and-tube exchangers, and to API RP 586 Part 1 for choosing tube inspection techniques.

The tube methods earlier in this article (ECT, IRIS, RFT, remote visual) are only part of an exchanger inspection. Under an API 510 programme, the exchanger is a pressure vessel with two pressure boundaries and two services, and the code's interval, repair and documentation rules apply to it. This section covers that code layer. It paraphrases API 510's eleventh edition (October 2022, with errata in 2023 and 2025, per API's announcement). Check the details against your licensed copy.

One correction to the standards list earlier in this article: API RP 578 is API's recommended practice for material verification programmes, meaning positive material identification. It is not an eddy current or remote-visual practice. It is still relevant to exchangers, because it guides alloy verification when tubes, tubesheets or channel parts are replaced. For tube technique selection, API 510 points to API RP 586 Part 1.

What API 510 says about heat exchangers

API 510's definition of a pressure vessel names heat exchangers, air coolers, columns, towers, unfired steam generators and other vapour-generating vessels heated indirectly. An exchanger in hydrocarbon or chemical process service is therefore inside the code's scope, unless it falls into one of the Annex A exemption classes, such as small-volume, low-pressure or small-diameter vessels.

The code then has a short clause on shell-and-tube exchangers (5.12 in the eleventh edition). It makes no exchanger-specific rules. It directs the reader to three documents:

  • API RP 572, the recommended practice on inspecting pressure vessels, which covers several exchanger types. Its fifth edition was published in November 2023.
  • ASME PCC-2, Article 312, on inspection and repair of shell-and-tube heat exchangers.
  • API RP 586, Part 1, on selecting heat exchanger tube inspection techniques.

Two other API 510 provisions matter for exchangers in particular. First, a vessel that by its design cannot be satisfactorily inspected internally or on-stream for its credible damage mechanisms must instead have analysis, monitoring and maintenance strategies to manage the risk of failure. The code gives an aluminum core exchanger as its example, and external inspection is still required. Second, the code allows a large vessel with zones that corrode at different rates to be handled zone by zone for interval setting. An exchanger's shell side and tube side often see completely different fluids, so the inspection plan should record the damage mechanisms and rates for each side separately.

How the tube bundle fits into the API 510 programme varies between owners. Some include tube inspection and plugging records in the API 510 vessel file. Others manage bundles under a separate reliability or bundle programme, with the API 510 file covering the shell, channel, covers, nozzles and tubesheet. Neither approach changes what the code expects for the pressure-retaining shell and channel. Whatever approach you use, write it into the QA manual and the inspection plan, and confirm with your jurisdiction if it regulates the exchanger.

Components, damage and API 510 scope: a working map

An exchanger inspection plan under API 510 normally lists every component, its likely damage and the examination that addresses it. The table is a typical starting map for a carbon steel shell-and-tube exchanger. Your own damage-mechanism review under API RP 571 decides what actually applies.

ComponentCommon damage to considerTypical examinations
Shell and shell nozzlesGeneral and localized corrosion; impingement opposite the inlet nozzle; CUI on insulated shells; cracking in amine, caustic or wet H2S servicesCML UT thickness; encoded corrosion mapping around inlets; external visual and CUI screening; WFMT or PAUT where cracking is credible
Channel, channel cover and bonnetUnder-deposit and cooling-water corrosion, MIC, galvanic attack at dissimilar joints; gasket-face damageVisual at bundle pull or cover removal; UT thickness and pit depth gauging; PT or MT of welds and cover attachment
Pass-partition platesThinning, erosion and distortion that cause pass bypassingVisual and UT; dimensional checks
TubesheetLigament cracking, tube-to-tubesheet joint leakage, crevice corrosion, cladding damageVisual; PT on tube-to-tubesheet welds; leak testing; UT for clad bond where relevant
TubesID and OD pitting, general wall loss, erosion at inlet ends, fretting at baffles, SCC, dezincification in some copper alloysECT, RFT, NFT, IRIS or tube MFL selected by material; tube pulls for metallurgical confirmation
Floating head cover and backing deviceCorrosion, bolting damage, gasket-face damageVisual, UT, bolting inspection
Air-cooler header boxes and plugsHeader corrosion, plug-hole thread and seat damage, tube-to-header leaksUT of header plates; visual of plug seats; NFT or IRIS of tubes

Choosing the tube technique by material

Tube inspection is where API 510 refers you to API RP 586 Part 1. In practice the tube material decides the technique first, and the damage mode second. The methods are described in more detail earlier in this article. This is the selection logic in brief:

  • Non-ferromagnetic tubes (austenitic stainless steel, copper alloys, titanium, some nickel alloys): conventional bobbin eddy current is the standard production method for pitting, wall loss and cracking indications. Array or rotating probes are used to characterise them.
  • Ferromagnetic tubes (carbon steel, ferritic stainless): remote field testing (RFT) screens for volumetric wall loss over the full tube length. Near field testing (NFT) is used for ID pitting in finned air-cooler tubes. Tube MFL is another option for ferromagnetic tubes.
  • Quantitative wall thickness on any material: IRIS ultrasonic testing gives a measured remaining wall and is often used to confirm and size electromagnetic calls. It needs clean tubes, a water fill and more time per tube.
  • Metallurgical confirmation: pulling one or more representative tubes for sectioning tests what the NDE calls assume, especially where SCC, dealloying or under-deposit attack is suspected.

What fraction of tubes to examine, how to choose them (inlet pass, high-velocity zones, known problem rows), and the plugging or retubing criteria are set by the owner's engineer and inspector. API 510 does not prescribe them. Record the sampling basis in the plan so the next inspection can trend against it.

Intervals for exchangers: the same rules, applied per side

Since the exchanger is a pressure vessel, API 510's interval rules apply. Unless RBI justifies otherwise, internal or on-stream inspection is due at the lesser of half the remaining life or 10 years. With less than four years of remaining life, the interval may be the full remaining life, up to two years. External inspection is due at the lesser of five years or the internal/on-stream interval. The inspector or engineer sets the intervals under the owner-operator's QA system.

In practice, exchanger inspections often happen earlier than the code ceiling. A bundle may be pulled for cleaning or for performance reasons such as fouling, pressure drop or leaks, and that gives access to the channel, shell interior and tubesheet. Most owners use these pulls to do the API 510 internal inspection, so the inspector should be told when one is planned.

On-stream substitution for an exchanger is limited by the code's conditions. Corrosion must be known to be low, remaining life must exceed 10 years, the service must be established for at least five years, there must be no cracking or hydrogen damage service and no loose liners, along with the other listed conditions. The same reasoning applies to the internal parts. An external survey of the shell says nothing about tubes, tubesheet or pass partitions. A plan that switches to on-stream inspection for the shell still needs a strategy for the tube side.

Repairs, plugging and testing under the API 510 framework

Exchanger work raises the same API 510 repair questions as any other vessel.

  • Authorization. Welding, cutting or grinding on pressure-containing parts (shell, channel, nozzles, tubesheet) is a repair or an alteration under API 510. The inspector must authorize it before the work starts, and the engineer must also authorize alterations. See API 510 repairs, alterations and rerating.
  • Tube plugging and retubing. ASME PCC-2 Article 312 gives guidance on exchanger repair. Material verification of replacement tubes and plugs follows the owner's PMI programme, with API RP 578 as the reference. A large number of plugged tubes changes the thermal and hydraulic design, so engineering review is needed as well as inspection.
  • Testing. A shell-side test is commonly used to find leaking tubes and tube-to-tubesheet joints. API 510's pressure-testing rules apply to the pressure boundaries after repair or alteration: a test is normally required after an alteration or major repair, and NDE may replace it only with the engineer's and inspector's approval. See API 510 pressure testing after repairs. For Type 300 series stainless steel parts, API 510 says to test with low-chloride water and to drain and dry afterwards.

A worked example, described qualitatively

Take a crude preheat exchanger with a carbon steel shell, carbon steel tubes and cooling water on the tube side in some passes. Pressure drop is rising, so the bundle is pulled for cleaning during a turnaround. The inspection plan treats this as the API 510 internal inspection for the shell and channel.

With the bundle out, the inspector does a visual inspection of the shell interior and channel. The examination crew re-measures the shell CMLs and maps the area opposite the inlet nozzle, where impingement is most likely. The channel has under-deposit pitting near the cooling-water inlet, which is gauged for depth. Because the tubes are carbon steel, RFT screens the full tube count selected in the plan. IRIS follows on a sample of the worst RFT indications to measure remaining wall, and one tube is pulled for metallurgical confirmation. The inspector evaluates the shell and channel data under API 510 and recalculates rates and remaining life. The owner's engineer reviews the tube data against the plugging criteria. Tubes are plugged, the channel pits are weld-repaired under an authorized repair plan with MT at the hold points, and the inspector sets the next due dates for each side.

Documentation and jurisdiction

  • An inspection plan listing both sides' damage mechanisms, CMLs, tube sampling basis, techniques and coverage.
  • Thickness and mapping data for the shell, channel and covers, with corrosion rates and remaining life per side.
  • Tube inspection data by tube location (a tubesheet map), with plugging history.
  • Repair plans, hold-point records, NDE reports, PMI records and any pressure test or substitution approval.

OSHA PSM-covered facilities treat these records as part of mechanical integrity. Some US jurisdictions register process exchangers under boiler and pressure vessel laws, and the National Board Inspection Code may apply to repairs there. In Canada, provincial regulators such as ABSA in Alberta set owner-user inspection (AB-506) and repair (AB-513) requirements. Confirm whether your exchanger is registered and what applies to it.

More questions on heat exchangers and API 510

Does API 510 cover heat exchangers?

Yes. API 510's definition of a pressure vessel includes heat exchangers and air coolers, unless they fall into an Annex A exemption class.

Does API 510 cover heat exchanger tube bundles?

The code covers the exchanger as a pressure vessel and refers tube inspection technique selection to API RP 586 Part 1, with inspection and repair guidance in API RP 572 and ASME PCC-2 Article 312. Owners differ on whether the bundle sits in the API 510 file or a separate bundle programme. Define it in your QA system.

What is the API 510 inspection interval for a heat exchanger?

The same as any vessel: internal or on-stream at the lesser of half the remaining life or 10 years, and external at the lesser of five years or the internal/on-stream interval, unless RBI justifies otherwise. Plan per side.

Which tube inspection method should be used for carbon steel tubes?

Usually RFT for full-length screening, NFT for finned air-cooler tubes, and IRIS to measure remaining wall at the worst indications. Eddy current suits non-ferromagnetic tubes.

Is shell and tube heat exchanger inspection covered by API RP 572?

Yes. API RP 572 supplements API 510 with inspection practices for several exchanger types, including air-cooled exchangers. The fifth edition was published in November 2023.
